checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: Two people type in the same paragraph at the same moment.

options.label: CRDTs
options.verdict: Genuinely elegant and it removes the need for a central server — which is why it wins for peer-to-peer and offline. The costs here are memory that only grows (tombstones are never removed) and conflict resolution that can read as untidy in plain text.

options.label: Operational Transformation
options.verdict: Each edit is transformed against the ops that preceded it, so both clients converge. It needs one server to order operations, which you already have, and it is low-memory and well suited to text.

defend.prompt: What does OT commit you to?

options.label: A central server that orders all operations
Transform logic on the client as well as the server
A bounded number of concurrent editors per document
Losing the ability to show live cursors

defend.explain: Cursors are ephemeral presence data and unaffected. OT buys low memory and good text behaviour at the cost of a central ordering point — which is exactly why the requirement caps concurrent editors.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Collaborative editing with a deliberate cap on concurrent editors.

rungs.note: Capping it is what makes central-server OT viable at all.
Under ~100ms, or typing feels laggy to collaborators.
Presence is ephemeral — it dies with the connection and is never persisted.

checkpoints.explain: The editor cap is the constraint that lets one server own ordering for a document. Remove it and you are forced toward CRDTs.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the edit path for a keystroke.
checkpoints.explain: All editors of a document must reach the same server, so the load balancer routes by document id — that consistent-hash decision is what makes central OT possible. Operations are appended durably before broadcast. Presence and compaction sit beside this path, not in it.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: Documents open slowly. Editing them, once open, is instant.
checkpoints.explain: Opening a document replays its entire operation log; editing only applies the newest op. A document with 2.1M un-compacted operations therefore takes seconds to open and microseconds to edit. Compaction — collapsing the log into a snapshot and flipping the version pointer — has stopped running.

wrong.OT Engine: 3ms per transform. It is fast; it is just being asked to do it two million times.
wrong.Redis presence: Presence is unrelated to document load time.
wrong.Load Balancer: Routing is healthy — the request reaches the right server quickly.
